source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
finding: Introduced GSM8K (8.5K problems) and the generate-many-then-rank-with-a-trained-verifier recipe. A verifier beats plain finetuning and scales better with data.
numbers: Verification gives about the same boost as a 30x larger model. Test@100: sample 100 completions, return the top verifier score. 6B verifier performance rises up to 400 completions per problem, then falls. With small training sets verification does not help; the 175B verifier takes off earlier than the 6B. Verifier gives a per-token value prediction by default.
quote: benefits of search are eventually outweighed by the risk of finding adversarial solutions that fool the verifier
limits: Only GSM8K; GPT-3 family models; final-answer labels only, so right-answer-wrong-reasoning is not penalised.
agent_relevance: Early direct evidence that more samples against a learned verifier can hurt after a point. Cap N and prefer code-checked selection (G5).

source: Uesato et al. (2022) Solving math word problems with process- and outcome-based feedback
finding: First careful process vs outcome comparison on GSM8K. Final-answer error is about the same for both; trace error (right answer, wrong reasoning) differs a lot.
numbers: Without reward model: 23.5% (outcome-based) vs 22.3% (process-based SFT) final-answer error. With reward-model reranking: 16.6% vs 14.8%. Best result 12.7% final-answer error (prior best 16.8%) and 3.4% trace error (prior 14.0%). Trace error: few-shot+final-answer RL 19.8% vs SFT 11.4%; with RM reranking 12.4% vs 4.4% (ORM) and 3.5% (PRM). RL against an ORM instead of raw final answer cuts trace error from 12.4% to 5.5%. With 30% abstention, final-answer error 2.7%. ORM predictions agree 85% with process labels but only 77% with outcome labels.
limits: GSM8K only, where wrong steps rarely give right answers. Authors warn the ORM-approximates-PRM effect may be dataset-specific. Trace error measured by human annotators on small samples (wide intervals, for example 3.7% with CI 0.5 to 6.9).
agent_relevance: A final-answer check alone lets wrong reasoning through. When the answer is checkable but the path matters, add a step check or a held-out test (G3).

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let us Verify Step by Step
finding: Human step-level labels (PRM800K, 800,000 labels) train a process reward model that beats outcome-supervised reward models on MATH.
numbers: Best-of-1860: PRM 78.2%, ORM 72.4%, majority vote 69.6% on a MATH test subset. PRM better at every data scale in best-of-500. Active learning (label the most convincing wrong solutions) is about 2.6x more data efficient than uniform labelling. Out of distribution, 234 STEM problems (AP Calc/Chem/Phys, AMC10/12) at best-of-100: PRM 72.9%, ORM 63.8%, majority 61.3%.
quote: process supervision significantly outperforms outcome supervision for training models to solve problems from the challenging MATH dataset
limits: Large GPT-4-based models; labels only up to the first error; the authors say final-answer false positives are probably over-emphasised in MATH and prefer PRM-large as the outcome baseline. Iterative retraining in active learning was unstable.
agent_relevance: Strongest case that step checking beats answer checking, but it needs about 800K human labels. We cannot train, so use it as a design argument only.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations
finding: Labels each step automatically by whether completions sampled from that step reach the right answer. Trains a PRM without humans.
numbers: Mistral-7B MetaMath: step-by-step PPO with the PRM raises GSM8K 77.9% to 84.1% and MATH 28.6% to 33.0%; with PRM verification on top 89.1% and 43.5%. Table 1, DeepSeek-67B: GSM8K self-consistency 88.2, ORM 92.6, Math-Shepherd 93.3, self-consistency+Math-Shepherd 92.5; MATH500 45.4, 45.3, 47.0, 48.1.
limits: A step counts as good if it can reach the right answer, so flawed steps that get lucky get credit. Gains over the ORM are small (about 0.7 to 2 points).
agent_relevance: Cheap way to get step labels without humans, but the label is an outcome estimate. See ProcessBench for its weakness.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction
finding: Train the verifier with the normal next-token loss so it can write a chain of thought before saying Yes/No, then vote over several verification chains.
numbers: Best-of-N with Gemma verifiers: algorithmic tasks 5% to 45.3%; GSM8K (Gemini 1.0 Pro solutions, Gemma2-9B verifier) 73% to 93.4%; MATH (trained on GSM8K only) 28% to 44.6%; MMLU abstract algebra 37.9% to 53.5%. Weighted self-consistency with GenRM-CoT needs 2.5x fewer solutions than with a discriminative RM. GenRM-CoT is 6.4x more sample efficient than discriminative verifiers on MATH. Beats LLM-as-a-judge that uses the stronger Gemini 1.0 Pro.
limits: Gains are against discriminative RMs and a prompted judge; GSM8K verification rationales were synthetic and can be wrong. Verifier token cost is not counted here (see Singhi).
agent_relevance: A verifier that reasons before judging is more accurate than a scalar score. Fits S8 VERIFY but only with a compute check.

source: Singhi et al. (2025) When To Solve, When To Verify: Compute-Optimal Problem Solving and Generative Verification
finding: Compute-matched test of self-consistency (SC) against a generative verifier with best-of-N. SC wins at most practical budgets.
numbers: GenRM first matches SC only after up to 8x the inference compute, and needs more to clearly beat it (MATH, Llama-3.1-8B). At a fixed number of solutions, GenRM-FT with 32 verifications matches SC with 4x fewer solutions, but that ignores verification cost. Fitted laws: optimal solutions S_opt ~ C^0.57, optimal verifications V_opt ~ C^0.39, so spend faster on solutions than on verifications. Hard problems gain up to 30% relative over SC. Also holds on AIME24 and GPQA-Diamond.
quote: SC is more compute-efficient than GenRM for most practical inference budgets
limits: Math and a few science tasks; verifier fine-tuned on MATH; compute counted as tokens proportional to FLOPs.
agent_relevance: At small budgets, vote first. Add a generative verifier only at large budgets or on hard items (G12).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) grows log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples. Where a perfect verifier exists, coverage becomes accuracy; where it does not, voting and reward models plateau.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250 samples), above the single-sample best of 43%. CodeContests Gemma-2B: 0.02% to 7.1% with 10,000 samples. MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% (100 samples) to 98.44% (10,000), but majority vote or reward model rise only from 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Coverage is an upper bound only with an oracle verifier. See next line for the verifier flaws the authors found.
agent_relevance: Verifier quality, not sample count, is the bottleneck for open-ended answers. Build executable checks wherever possible (G3).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys, section 4.2 verifier imperfections
finding: Even execution-based verifiers are imperfect: test suites can be flaky, reject correct answers, or accept wrong ones.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 11.3% of problems have flaky test suites that sometimes fail even the gold patch. CodeContests: of 122 test problems with Python3 solutions, 35 have listed correct solutions that fail the tests (multiple valid outputs not handled, malformed mutated inputs).
limits: One benchmark each; counts come from the authors' own re-run of reference solutions.
agent_relevance: Run each check more than once and treat inconsistent results as no signal. Test the checker on known-good answers first.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: If the verifier has a non-zero false-positive rate, resampling until it passes has an accuracy ceiling no budget can lift. Weaker models have higher false-positive rates, so they cannot catch up with stronger ones.
numbers: HumanEval+ (200+ samples per task, 1,000 for Command Light) and MBPP+ (50 per task), weaker original tests as verifier: false-positive probability rises linearly as true single-sample accuracy falls, across Cohere Command, GPT-4o and Llama-3.1 families. With a cost for false positives, the optimal number of attempts is often below 10 (for example about 5 or fewer) and can be zero if a wrong answer costs more than a right one gains. False positives also have worse style on all four readability metrics.
quote: Resampling cannot decrease this probability, so it imposes an upper bound
limits: Code only; the cost-benefit ratio is assumed, not measured. Task difficulty is bimodal, which drives the rising false-positive rate at high K.
agent_relevance: Keep attempts per item small and give a false pass a cost. Never score success with the same tests used to select (G3).

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Reported self-correction gains came from oracle labels that told the model when to stop. Without the oracle, a model judging its own answer gets worse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: standard 75.9, with oracle labels 84.3 (GPT-4: 95.5 to 97.5); GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correct round 1 = 75.1, round 2 = 74.7. CommonSenseQA GPT-3.5 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 to 90.0. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5 to 36.5. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time and changes correct answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 era; prompts follow the source papers; HotpotQA sample is 100. Later RL-trained reasoning models may judge differently.
agent_relevance: Backs G2: no revision from the model's own opinion. Use output from code or an external check.

source: Huang et al. (2023), debate versus voting at equal responses
finding: Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at equal numbers of model responses.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: self-consistency 82.5 (3 responses), 85.3 (6), 88.2 (9). Multi-agent debate 83.2 (3 responses, round 1) and 83.0 (9 responses, round 2). One-response baseline 76.7.
limits: GSM8K only; GPT-3.5; table in the text copy is hard to align, so values are the best reading of the layout.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 (no debate). Spend extra calls on independent samples.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 as its own verifier has many false negatives, so an LLM+LLM loop does worse than no loop. A sound external verifier gives large gains and the critique text barely matters.
numbers: GPT-4 as verifier: Game of 24 accuracy 87.0% (3567/4100), false-positive rate 10.4%, false-negative rate 20.7%; graph coloring accuracy 72.4%, FPR 6.5%, FNR 95.8% (113/118); Blocksworld 71.8%, FPR 18.55%, FNR 15.48%; Mystery Blocksworld 79.6%, FPR 0.5%, FNR 97.09% (100/103). Game of 24 standard prompting 5%; with a sound verifier and feedback about 36 to 38%. Chain-of-thought lifted Game of 24 verification accuracy from 87% to 98.8%. Majority vote of 15 gave no gain over standard prompting.
limits: 100 instances per domain; GPT-4 only; the table text is garbled, so only cells that matched the narrative are used.
agent_relevance: A verifier with 95% false negatives rejects correct work and sends the loop to worse guesses. Measure a verifier's false-negative rate before trusting it (G5, G6).

source: Stechly et al. (2024), sound verifier versus critique content
finding: Most of the gain from an external verifier comes from getting more guesses checked, not from the critique content.
numbers: Three feedback levels (binary, first error, all errors) gave similar gains. Resampling with the same prompt until a sound verifier passed matched them at lower token cost, since prompts do not grow with iteration.
limits: 100 instances per domain; GPT-4.
agent_relevance: A cheap pass/fail from code plus independent resamples may be as good as elaborate critique. Fits S5: revise from real output but keep it short.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: Measured position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement bias and weak math grading in LLM judges. GPT-4 still agrees with humans at 85% (no ties).
numbers: Position consistency when answer order is swapped (default prompt): Claude-v1 23.8%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, GPT-4 65.0%. Verbosity 'repetitive list' attack: judge fooled in 91.3% of 23 cases for Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5, 8.7% for GPT-4. GPT-4 favours itself by about 10 points of win rate and Claude-v1 by 25, but the authors say data are too limited to confirm self-enhancement. Math grading, judge failed 14/20 with default prompt, 6/20 with chain-of-thought, 3/20 with a reference answer. GPT-4 vs human agreement 85% (non-tie); human vs human 81%.
limits: 58 expert annotators on MT-bench; chat questions; 2023 judge models; the self-enhancement result is weak.
agent_relevance: Mitigations that work: swap order and call a tie if verdicts differ; give the judge a reference answer; make it reason first. Fits G5.

source: Zheng et al. (2023), judge reliability by case type
finding: Judge agreement with humans rises with the quality gap between answers. On math and coding questions judges are more confident even when wrong.
numbers: GPT-4 and human agreement increases with the win-rate gap of the model pair (Figure 2); position bias is more noticeable on open questions such as writing and humanities than on math and coding.
limits: Read from text and figure captions; no table copied.
agent_relevance: Never use an LLM judge for exact-answer tasks that code can check.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Models can recognise their own text, and the stronger the self-recognition, the stronger the self-preference. Fine-tuning shows a linear link and control runs argue for a causal role.
numbers: Out of the box all three LLMs beat 50% at telling their own output from other sources; GPT-4 is 73.5% accurate separating itself from two other LLMs and humans. Fine-tuning on 500 examples gives over 90% self-recognition for GPT-3.5 and Llama 2. Self-preference is linearly related to self-recognition (CNN/DailyMail). Reversing source labels flips GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 preference on XSUM, but not on CNN/DM or for Llama.
limits: Summarisation only (XSUM, CNN/DM); fine-tuned evaluators; label-swap effect missing on CNN/DM.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G5: hide authorship from any model judge, since it may recognise its own text.

source: Shi et al. (2024) Judging the Judges: A Systematic Study of Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Large study of position bias: 15 judges, MTBench and DevBench, 22 tasks, about 40 generators, over 150,000 evaluations. Bias is not random, varies by judge and task, and depends mainly on the quality gap between answers.
numbers: Defines repetition stability, position consistency and preference fairness. Significant factors by stepwise regression: judge identity, candidate identity, task category. Prompt length has a weak effect. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-Turbo prefer the later answer on MTBench but the earlier on DevBench.
limits: Exploratory study; judge versions change fast.
agent_relevance: A pairwise judge is least reliable when the options are close, which is when selection matters. Use both orders and require agreement.

source: Gao, Schulman, Hilton (2022) Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
finding: With a gold reward model standing in for humans, optimising a proxy reward model first helps, then hurts, the gold score. Functional forms are fitted for best-of-n and for RL.
numbers: Gold score vs d = sqrt(KL from the start): best-of-n R = d(alpha - beta d); RL R = d(alpha - beta log d). Coefficients change smoothly, about logarithmically, with reward-model parameters. Policy size has weak effect on the amount of overoptimization. KL penalty gave no measurable gold-reward gain at a given KL. RL is slower than best-of-n per unit KL.
limits: Synthetic gold RM, InstructGPT setup, 1.2B policy in the main figures; the authors flag the KL-penalty result as hyperparameter sensitive.
agent_relevance: Cleanest model of why more selection pressure on a learned judge eventually hurts. Reason to cap N and prefer checks the answer cannot game.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Test-time search against a process verifier works differently by question difficulty. The best compute split depends on the difficulty bin.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation improves efficiency over best-of-N by more than 4x. In a FLOPs-matched comparison with a 14x larger model, the smaller model with test-time compute wins on easy and medium questions under some conditions. Beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets but falls below it at large budgets. On MATH levels 1-2 beam search gets worse as budget grows; on levels 3-4 it beats best-of-N; on level 5 nothing makes much progress. The authors found PRM800K labels ineffective for their PaLM 2 model (easy to exploit with best-of-N) and used Monte Carlo step labels.
quote: on the easy questions (levels 1 and 2), the stronger optimizer of the two approaches, beam search, degrades performance
limits: PaLM 2 on MATH; difficulty bins by oracle or by model prediction; PRM trained on rollouts.
agent_relevance: Spend by difficulty (G12). A stronger search against a learned verifier hurts on easy items, so skip it there.

source: Snell et al. (2024), compute-optimal verifier search with predicted difficulty
finding: Choosing the search method per difficulty bin is the main gain.
numbers: With oracle difficulty bins, compute-optimal search matches best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute (for example 16 versus 64 generations). With model-predicted bins some benefit stays at low budgets and shrinks at high budgets.
limits: Needs a difficulty estimate, which costs inference; two-fold cross validation used for the bins.
agent_relevance: Supports S0 GATE and G12: classify the item first, then pick how much to verify.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: 3,400 expert-annotated solutions to test whether a model can find the first wrong step. Open PRMs trained on automatic labels generalise badly; prompted critic models do better.
numbers: F1 on GSM8K / MATH / OlympiadBench: Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B 47.9 / 29.5 / 24.8; Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K 68.2 / 62.6 / 50.7; GPT-4o-0806 79.2 / 63.6 / 51.4 (average 61.9); o1-mini 93.2 / 88.9 / 87.2 (average 87.9). QwQ-32B-Preview average 71.5, competitive with GPT-4o. All models drop as problems get harder.
quote: Existing PRMs typically fail to generalize to more challenging math problems beyond GSM8K and MATH
limits: Math only; the table text is partly garbled, so only the listed cells are used.
agent_relevance: Step-level checking ability tracks base-model strength; small trained PRMs are weak on hard items. A strong prompted critic may beat a trained PRM.

source: Hosseini et al. (2024) V-STaR: Training Verifiers for Self-Taught Reasoners
finding: Train a DPO verifier on both correct and wrong generated solutions and iterate with the generator. Best-of-64 with the verifier beats self-improvement and plain verification.
numbers: LLaMA2 7B and 13B: 4% to 17% absolute accuracy gain over baselines; 6 to 17 points in math over STaR and Verification, 4 to 12 in code. Gains grow more across verifier iterations than generator iterations. A 4th iteration on MBPP adds 0.3%. Out-of-domain (MBPP to HumanEval; GSM8K to a 150-problem MATH level-1 subset) gains hold but are smaller.
limits: Small LLaMA2 models; the MATH subset is only 150 easy problems.
agent_relevance: Wrong attempts carry information that correct-only filtering throws away. Keep failed attempts as negative evidence for selection.

source: Chen et al. (2022) CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
finding: Have the same model write tests, run all codes on all tests, and pick the largest consensus set of codes that pass the same tests (dual execution agreement).
numbers: code-davinci-002 pass@1: HumanEval 47.0 to 65.8 (+18.8), MBPP 58.1 to 67.7, APPS Introductory 27.2 to 34.6, CodeContests 0.7 to 2.1. Previous best on HumanEval 42.7. Codex code-cushman-001: pass@100 77.4% but pass@1 33.5%.
limits: Samples and tests come from one model, so wrong code and wrong tests can agree. CodeContests gain is small in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: Model-written tests are a cheap check but not independent evidence (G4). Prefer tests from the problem statement or held-out cases (G3).

source: Survey on verifiers for test-time scaling (arXiv 2508.16665)
finding: Survey of verifier types: prompt-based, discriminative (outcome or process), generative, symbolic or tool-based; trained by SFT, RL or self-training.
numbers: Taxonomy table lists discriminative ORMs and PRMs (for example Math-Shepherd), generative verifiers (Zhang 2024a, GenRM Mahan 2024) marked outcome or process, and reasoning-based generative verifiers. Says discriminative verifiers have poor robustness and can learn spurious correlations; generative verifiers can use chain of thought and votes.
limits: Only the taxonomy text was read, not every cited result; no measured numbers of its own in the parts read.
agent_relevance: A map for choices: our S4 uses a symbolic check, S8 could use a generative verifier.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys, section 4.1 voting versus reward models
finding: Majority vote cannot find a rare correct answer because it picks the most common one. Success saturates near 100 samples while coverage keeps rising.
numbers: Three selectors on GSM8K and MATH with Llama-3-8B/70B-Instruct and 10,000 samples per problem: majority vote, reward-model best-of-N, reward-model-weighted vote (ArmoRM-Llama3-8B). All plateau near 100 samples; coverage exceeds 95%. The gap between oracle coverage and any practical selector grows with samples.
quote: the occurrence of rare, correct solutions does not affect the most common answer that majority voting chooses
limits: Only one reward model; GSM8K and MATH subsets.
agent_relevance: Voting has a ceiling set by how often the right answer is the mode. When the right answer is rare, a real check is needed, not agreement.

source: Uesato et al. (2022), RM reranking versus RM inside RL
finding: Reward-model feedback used inside RL cuts trace error most. Reranking with an RM also cuts it.
numbers: SFT trace error with RM reranking 4.4% (ORM) and 3.5% (PRM) vs 11.4% without reranking; few-shot RL with ORM reaches 5.5% trace error vs 12.4% with final-answer RL plus ORM reranking.
limits: Intervals are wide; GSM8K only.
agent_relevance: Watch the reasoning path, not only the last line, wherever the answer check is easy to satisfy by luck.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021), verifier training details and test-time compute
finding: Verifier training choices matter: token-level value head by default, a joint generation objective as auxiliary loss, dropout as a strong regulariser, and voting among top-ranked solutions for more gain.
numbers: Default evaluation uses 100 completions because it captures most of the gain at modest cost; search benefit peaks at 400 completions for the 6B verifier.
limits: Exact top-k voting numbers were not read from the figure text.
agent_relevance: Combining a verifier score with a vote is the usual practical form; later papers confirm weighted voting.
